one_liner: Ruby 1.9.3 subset on PyPy's RPython meta-tracing JIT; in one shootout beats CRuby 2.7.7 on 12 of 13 programs.
what_it_does: Topaz is a Ruby interpreter written in RPython and translated with `rpython -Ojit targettopaz.py` into a standalone `bin/topaz` binary that you run like `ruby file.rb`. It targets Ruby 1.9.3 and is explicitly 'extremely incomplete': most of the standard library, threads, call/cc, `private` visibility, flip-flops and `if /regex/` are missing. The measured build is kostya/topaz, a benchmark-oriented fork that builds on PyPy 2.7 v7.3.x; upstream was last developed in 2017.
how_it_is_fast: RPython generates a meta-tracing JIT from the bytecode interpreter (a JitDriver with greens pc/bytecode/block_bytecode, `jit.promote` on receiver classes and lexical scopes), plus RPython's generational GC, so hot loops become specialised machine code with boxed integers and floats removed. Objects use SELF-style maps with type-specialised instance variables that store Fixnum and Float fields unboxed. The measured fork also replaces the RPython OrderedDict behind Hash with a simpler hash-to-index-list table (commit claims 8x faster get/set) and streams file reads.
when_to_use: Research or teaching on meta-tracing JITs: a compact example of a dynamic-language VM built on RPython.

Self-contained numeric or object-allocation Ruby scripts (nbody, mandelbrot, matmul, spectralnorm, binarytrees style) that use only core Ruby 1.9 classes, where it ran 3.4x-12x faster than CRuby 2.7.7.
Batch Ruby jobs under a tight memory budget where JRuby or TruffleRuby cost hundreds of MB to GBs: Topaz used about 27-116 MB on 11 of 13 shootout programs.
Long-running loops where JIT warm-up is amortised over several iterations in one process.
when_not_to_use: Any real application or gem: Ruby 1.9.3 only, most of the stdlib and many builtin methods missing, no Rails, no C extensions, no threads.

Production use: upstream calls itself not stable and untested in the real world, issue #841 'Is this project dead?' (2015) went unanswered, and the last upstream code change is a 2022 one-line fix after 2017.
String-transform and IO-heavy work: revcomp ran 7.3 s vs CRuby 2.7.7 4.2 s and Ruby 3.2.1 3.67 s, using 787.5 MB vs 164.4 MB.
Code relying on Hash#compare_by_identity or heavy hash deletion when using the measured kostya fork (see gotchas).
Windows: upstream says it is untested there.

integration.form: standalone executable (RPython-translated bin/topaz); not an embeddable library
integration.dependencies: PyPy source tree for the RPython toolchain (upstream README: PyPy tag release-2.4.0; kostya fork: pypy2.7 v7.3.2 in its Dockerfile, v7.3.6 in the shootout), a Python 2.7/PyPy2 host to run translation, rply, libffi-dev, gcc
integration.min_toolchain: Python 2.7 / PyPy2 host; translation takes 5-10 minutes; the shootout Dockerfile notes the fork compiles only with pypy2.7-v7.3.6
integration.platforms: Linux and macOS tested upstream; Windows untested; the shootout builds the fork on x86_64 and aarch64
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same `topaz file.rb` command line as `ruby file.rb`, but only for programs inside its Ruby 1.9.3 subset

gotchas: The shootout times the kostya/topaz fork (cloned at HEAD, unpinned), not this repository; upstream lacks the fork's hash and file-read speedups and pins PyPy 2.4.0, so it will likely not build on current PyPy and may be slower on knucleotide, fasta and other hash or IO programs.

The fork's speed-up came with semantic loss: Hash#compare_by_identity and compare_by_identity? are commented out (17 rubyspec tags in spec/tags/core/hash/compare_by_identity_tags.txt), and its OrderedHash never compacts deleted entries (rebuild() is a no-op), so deletes leave tombstones and repeated Hash#shift rescans them from the start.

Harness flaw favouring JITs: 'Runs' are in-process iterations of one launch and the table reports the best one, so Topaz shows a warm-JIT best of 5 while CRuby 2.7.7 finished only 1 iteration of brainfuck (115.31 s) and 2 of brainfuck2 within the timeout; startup is excluded.
Topaz can use more memory than CRuby on string-heavy programs: regexdna 298.9 MB vs 112.5 MB, revcomp 787.5 MB vs 164.4 MB.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Against JRuby (faster than CRuby on 9 of 13 programs in the same shootout but using about 370 MB-2.1 GB per run) and the shootout's TruffleRuby rows (faster than Topaz on 8 of 13, e.g. nbody 0.85 s vs 5.42 s, with 330 MB-2.8 GB), Topaz wins only on knucleotide, regexdna and revcomp among the JITs and on memory (about 27-120 MB on most programs); pick it only for code inside its Ruby 1.9.3 subset where footprint matters, and use JRuby or TruffleRuby for any real Ruby program.
verified_claims_summary: In kostya/jit-benchmarks round 1 (2023-02-28, AMD Ryzen 7 3800X, Docker on Ubuntu 22.10), the kostya/topaz fork translated with RPython from PyPy 2.7 v7.3.6 beat CRuby 2.7.7p221 (gcc 12.2.0 build) on 12 of 13 Benchmarks-Game-style programs, from 1.5x on pidigits (7.78 s vs 11.42 s) to about 10x on fannkuchredux and 12x on spectralnorm (derived from page data), and lost on revcomp (7.3 s vs 4.2 s). Times are the best in-process iteration measured by each program, so JIT warm-up and startup are excluded.
status_note: Abandoned: upstream development stopped in 2017 (one 2022 fix) and the benchmarked fork's last commit is 2023-01-27; BSD-3-Clause and pure RPython, but it needs an old PyPy2 toolchain to build and only runs a subset of Ruby 1.9.3, so it is a research artefact rather than a usable Ruby.
